items.prose: You roll a fair die three times.
items.question: What is the chance all three rolls are different? Give a fraction.

widget.label: Chance, as a fraction
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{5}{9}$, such as $\tfrac{120}{216}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the ordered rolls with no repeat, over all $6^3$ ordered rolls.

byKey.repeats: You counted every roll as different. Rolls like (2, 2, 5) repeat a face.
byKey.unordered: You counted unordered sets of faces, $\binom{6}{3} = 20$, over ordered rolls. Use ordered counts on both lines.
byKey.one-pair: That is the chance the first two rolls differ. The third must differ from both.

explain.text: All $6^3 = 216$ ordered rolls are equally likely. Rolls with no repeat: $6 \times 5 \times 4 = 120$. So the chance is $\tfrac{120}{216} = \tfrac{5}{9}$.

items.prose: Nine traders each shake hands once with every other trader.
items.question: How many handshakes are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A handshake is an unordered pair of two different traders.

byKey.ordered: You counted A with B and B with A. That is one handshake, so halve it.
byKey.square: You counted a trader shaking their own hand, and each pair twice.
byKey.nine: That counts traders. Each one shakes 8 hands, and each handshake has two people.

explain.text: Each handshake is a pair of traders, with no order. There are $9 \times 8 = 72$ ordered pairs, each handshake twice. So $\binom{9}{2} = 36$.

items.prose: A bag holds 4 red and 6 blue balls. You draw two without replacement.
items.question: What is the chance both balls are the same colour? Give a fraction.

widget.label: Chance, as a fraction
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{7}{15}$, such as $\tfrac{42}{90}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two paths: red then red, and blue then blue.

byKey.replaced: That is $0.4^2 + 0.6^2$, which puts the first ball back.
byKey.red-only: That is red then red only. Blue then blue is also the same colour.
byKey.fixed: You kept 10 balls for the second draw. Only 9 are left.

explain.text: Red, red: $\tfrac{4}{10} \times \tfrac{3}{9} = \tfrac{12}{90}$. Blue, blue: $\tfrac{6}{10} \times \tfrac{5}{9} = \tfrac{30}{90}$. The two paths cannot both happen, so add: $\tfrac{42}{90} = \tfrac{7}{15}$.

items.prose: A desk shares 9 identical bonus units of £1,000 among 3 traders. Each trader gets at least one unit.
items.question: How many ways can the units be shared?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put 2 bars into the 8 gaps between 9 stars.

byKey.empty-allowed: That is $\binom{11}{2}$, which lets a trader get nothing.
byKey.distinct: That is $3^9$, as if the units were different. Only the amounts matter.
byKey.nine-gaps: Nine stars have 8 gaps between them, not 9.

explain.text: Each trader needs at least one unit, so the 2 bars go in different gaps between the 9 stars. There are 8 gaps, so $\binom{8}{2} = 28$ sharings.

items.prose: Each choice below picks 3 items from 10.
items.question: Which are counted by $\binom{10}{3} = 120$? Select all that apply.

options.text: Gold, silver and bronze for 3 of 10 strategies
options.why: The medals differ, so order matters: $10 \times 9 \times 8 = 720$.

options.text: A 3-digit code where digits may repeat
options.why: Order matters and repeats are allowed: $10^3 = 1000$.

feedback.correct: The basket and the committee ignore order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether swapping two chosen items gives a different outcome.

explain.text: The basket and the committee stay the same when two members swap, so $\binom{10}{3}$ counts them. The podium keeps order: 720. The code allows repeats and keeps order: 1000.

items.prose: You draw a card from a 52-card deck, put it back and shuffle, then draw again.
items.question: What is the chance both cards are aces? Give a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With replacement, the second draw sees the full deck again.

byKey.without: That is the chance without replacement. Here the first card goes back.
byKey.added: You added the chances. Both draws must be aces, so multiply.

explain.text: Putting the card back restores 4 aces in 52 cards. The draws are independent, so multiply: $\tfrac{4}{52} \times \tfrac{4}{52} = \tfrac{1}{169}$.

items.prose: Four funds receive whole numbers of identical units, $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + x_4 = 6$, each $x_i \ge 0$.
items.question: How many solutions are there?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use 6 stars and 3 bars.

byKey.k-bars: You used 4 bars. Four funds need 3 bars.
byKey.no-bar-places: You chose 3 of 6 places. The bars add 3 places: 9.
byKey.distinct: That is $4^6$, as if the units were different.
byKey.at-least-one: That forces every $x_i \ge 1$. Zero is allowed here.

explain.text: Each solution is a row of 6 stars and 3 bars. Choosing the 3 bar places of 9 gives $\binom{9}{3} = 84$.

items.prose: You are dealt 5 cards from a shuffled 52-card deck, every hand equally likely.
items.question: What is the chance all 5 are hearts? Give a fraction.

widget.label: Chance, as a fraction
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{33}{66640}$, such as $\tfrac{1287}{2598960}$, about 0.000495.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count hands of 5 hearts over all hands of 5, both unordered.

byKey.replaced: That is $(\tfrac{1}{4})^5$, which puts each card back. Hearts run down as you deal.
byKey.mixed: You counted heart hands unordered but all hands in order. Use the same kind of count on both lines.

explain.text: Heart hands: $\binom{13}{5} = 1287$. All hands: $\binom{52}{5} = 2{,}598{,}960$. So the chance is $\tfrac{33}{66640} \approx 0.0005$, the same as $\tfrac{13}{52}\cdot\tfrac{12}{51}\cdot\tfrac{11}{50}\cdot\tfrac{10}{49}\cdot\tfrac{9}{48}$.
